lead: The convolution integral gives the output of a continuous-time LTI system from its input x(t) and its impulse response h(t): y(t)=x(t)*h(t). It adds up one shifted, scaled copy of h for every instant of the input. To evaluate it, flip h, slide it across x, multiply the two where they overlap and take the area. Engineers use it to predict a filter's response to a pulse, a loudspeaker's response to a click and a channel's response to one data symbol.
prereq: You need: linear time-invariant (LTI) systems and impulse response and step response.

sections.h3: From shifted impulses to an integral

blocks.text: Cut the input into narrow strips of width Δτ. The strip at time τ is close to an impulse of area x(τ)Δτ placed at τ. By time invariance and scaling the system answers it with x(τ)Δτ·h(t−τ). By additivity the output is the sum of all these answers. As Δτ→0 the sum becomes an integral:

blocks.where: t is the output time (s), the instant at which you want y; τ is the dummy integration variable (s) that runs along the input's past and future; x(τ) is the input; h(t−τ) is the impulse response flipped and slid to t; y(t) is the output. The integral is also called the superposition integral.

blocks.text: Two common cases shorten the limits. If the system is causal, h(t−τ)=0 whenever t−τ<0, that is whenever τ>t, so the upper limit becomes t. If the input starts at zero, x(τ)=0 for τ<0, so the lower limit becomes 0. With both, y(t)=∫<sub>0</sub><sup>t</sup> x(τ)h(t−τ)dτ for t≥0. Use this short form only when both conditions hold.
Graphical convolution is a five-step routine. It turns the integral into areas you can see, and it shows where the limits come from.

items: Sketch x(τ) on a τ axis.
Sketch h(τ) and flip it about τ=0 to get h(−τ).
Slide the flipped copy right by t to get h(t−τ); its right edge sits at τ=t.
Multiply x(τ) by h(t−τ) at every τ.
Integrate the product over the overlap only. Repeat for each range of t in which the overlap has the same shape.

blocks.text: The edges of the overlap change at breakpoints: values of t where an edge of h(t−τ) crosses an edge of x(τ). Each range between breakpoints is a separate case with its own limits. In the worked example x lasts from 0 to 2 s and h starts at 0, so the breakpoints are t=0 and t=2 s: for 0≤t<2 s the overlap is 0≤τ≤t, and for t≥2 s it is 0≤τ≤2.

Some syllabi ask for numerical convolution: sample the integrand and add areas. At t=1 s in the worked example the integrand is f(τ)=e<sup>τ−1</sup> on 0≤τ≤1. With step 0.5 s the samples at τ=0, 0.5, 1 are 0.3679, 0.6065 and 1.0000. The trapezoid rule gives 0.5×[0.5(0.3679+1.0000)+0.6065]=0.6452. The exact value is 0.6321, so the error is 0.0131; halving the step to 0.25 s gives 0.6354, an error of 0.0033. A quick numerical check like this catches sign slips in exponents, because a wrong sign changes the answer by far more than the rule's error.

examples.question: Let x(t)=u(t)−u(t−2) (a 2 s unit pulse) and h(t)=e<sup>−t</sup>u(t), t in seconds. Find y(t)=x(t)*h(t) for all t, and give y(1), y(2) and y(3) to three decimal places.
steps: Set up: y(t)=∫x(τ)h(t−τ)dτ. Here x(τ)=1 for 0≤τ<2 and 0 elsewhere. h(t−τ)=e<sup>−(t−τ)</sup> when t−τ≥0, that is when τ≤t, and 0 otherwise.
The product is nonzero only where 0≤τ<2 and τ≤t. Breakpoints: t=0 and t=2 s. Cases: t<0, 0≤t<2, t≥2.
Case t<0: the flipped h lies entirely left of τ=0 and does not reach the pulse, so y(t)=0.

Case 0≤t<2: the overlap is 0≤τ≤t. y(t)=∫<sub>0</sub><sup>t</sup>e<sup>−(t−τ)</sup>dτ=e<sup>−t</sup>∫<sub>0</sub><sup>t</sup>e<sup>τ</sup>dτ=e<sup>−t</sup>(e<sup>t</sup>−1)=1−e<sup>−t</sup>. So y(1)=1−e<sup>−1</sup>=1−0.368=0.632.

Case t≥2: the overlap is the whole pulse, 0≤τ≤2. y(t)=∫<sub>0</sub><sup>2</sup>e<sup>−(t−τ)</sup>dτ=e<sup>−t</sup>(e<sup>2</sup>−1)=e<sup>2−t</sup>−e<sup>−t</sup>. So y(2)=1−e<sup>−2</sup>=1−0.135=0.865 and y(3)=e<sup>−1</sup>−e<sup>−3</sup>=0.368−0.050=0.318.

Check continuity at the breakpoint: the first case gives 1−e<sup>−2</sup>=0.865 at t=2 and the second gives e<sup>0</sup>−e<sup>−2</sup>=0.865. The pieces join, as they must when neither signal contains an impulse.

traps: The limits come from the overlap, not automatically 0 to t. In the worked example the upper limit stays at 2 for every t≥2 s.
h(t−τ)=e<sup>−(t−τ)</sup>=e<sup>−t+τ</sup>, not e<sup>−t−τ</sup>. Writing the wrong sign gives y(1)=e<sup>−1</sup>(1−e<sup>−1</sup>)=0.233 instead of 0.632.
Flip one signal only. In ∫x(τ)h(t−τ)dτ it is h that is flipped; flipping both, or neither, is a different integral.
Missing a case: for two finite pulses there are usually four or five ranges of t (no overlap, entering, full, leaving, no overlap). Write the case for t<0 and the last case too.
The output does not stop when the input stops. For t>2 s, x(t)=0 but y(t)=e<sup>2−t</sup>−e<sup>−t</sup>≠0, because the system remembers the past input.

quiz.q: Write the convolution integral and name each symbol.
quiz.a: y(t)=∫<sub>−∞</sub><sup>∞</sup>x(τ)h(t−τ)dτ: t is the output time, τ the dummy integration variable, x the input, h the impulse response and y the output.

quiz.q: Why is τ called a dummy variable?
quiz.a: It exists only inside the integral; once the integral is evaluated τ disappears and the result depends on t alone.

quiz.q: Why does a causal h(t) let you replace the upper limit ∞ by t?
quiz.a: Causal means h(t)=0 for t<0, so h(t−τ)=0 whenever τ>t. The integrand is zero above τ=t, so integrating beyond t adds nothing.

quiz.q: Let x(t)=u(t)−u(t−1) and h(t)=e<sup>−t</sup>u(t). Find y(t) for 0≤t<1 and t≥1, and give y(0.5) and y(1).
quiz.a: For 0≤t<1: y=∫<sub>0</sub><sup>t</sup>e<sup>−(t−τ)</sup>dτ=1−e<sup>−t</sup>, so y(0.5)=0.393. For t≥1: y=∫<sub>0</sub><sup>1</sup>e<sup>−(t−τ)</sup>dτ=e<sup>1−t</sup>−e<sup>−t</sup>, so y(1)=1−0.368=0.632.

quiz.q: x(t)=1 for 0≤t≤2 s and 0 elsewhere; h(t)=2 for 0≤t≤1 s and 0 elsewhere. Find y(0.5), y(1.5) and y(2.5).
quiz.a: y equals 2 × (length of overlap). For 0≤t<1, y=2t, so y(0.5)=1. For 1≤t<2 the overlap is 1 s, so y(1.5)=2. For 2≤t<3, y=2(3−t), so y(2.5)=1.

quiz.q: A student writes y(t)=∫<sub>0</sub><sup>t</sup>x(τ)h(t+τ)dτ. Find the mistake and write the correct form for causal h and x(t)=0 for t<0.
quiz.a: The argument of h must be t−τ (flip and slide), not t+τ. Correct: y(t)=∫<sub>0</sub><sup>t</sup>x(τ)h(t−τ)dτ for t≥0, and y(t)=0 for t<0.

quiz.q: In the worked example, explain why y(t) is largest at t=2 s.
quiz.a: Until t=2 s more of the pulse enters the overlap, so y rises. After t=2 s no new input arrives and the weights e<sup>−(t−τ)</sup> on the old input shrink, so y falls. The peak is where the input ends: y(2)=0.865.

beyond: Not for the exam. Convolution reverb in audio software convolves a dry recording with a measured room impulse response. Image blur and sharpening are two-dimensional convolutions with a small kernel. Long convolutions are computed with the fast Fourier transform, because convolution in time is multiplication in frequency, as the convolution theorem of Fourier analysis shows. Search for "convolution reverb" and "FFT convolution overlap-add".

figure.caption: Graphical convolution of the 2 s pulse x(τ) with h(t−τ)=e<sup>−(t−τ)</sup> for τ ≤ t. The shaded overlap area is the output: 0.632 at t=1 s and 0.318 at t=3 s. The bottom plot joins all such areas into y(t), which peaks at 0.865 when the pulse ends at t=2 s.

spec.aria: Two rows show the pulse from 0 to 2 and the flipped exponential ending at tau equals t, for t equals 1 and 3 seconds, with the overlap shaded. The bottom plot shows y(t) rising to 0.865 at 2 s and decaying, with y(1)=0.632 and y(3)=0.318.
